title: Geometric-stalk perfectness at finite and field coefficients
statement:
Let $\Lambda=A_{E,n}$, let $M\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$ be a
bounded constructible
complex of finite Tor amplitude
on the coefficient site,
and let $\bar y\to Y$ be a
geometric point.
Then $M_{\bar y}\in D(\Lambda)$ is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded
complex of finite free $\Lambda$-modules. The same conclusion
holds on the small etale site with the corresponding constructibility
and derived-tensor
Tor-amplitude conditions.
Separately, for a bounded constructible complex at a
field coefficient stage
$E$, or in the
common-stage
$\Qlb$-category, its geometric stalk is a bounded complex of
finite-dimensional vector spaces over that field and is perfect.

proof.text: For finite coefficients write $C=M_{\bar y}$. On the pro-etale site use the pointed weakly etale stalk of [def-weil-proetale-geometric-stalk], whose exactness is [lem-cbc-proetale-classical-stalk]; on the small etale site use [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks] and [prop-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks-exact]. Exactness identifies $H^i(C)$ with $\mathcal H^i(M)_{\bar y}$. Each is finite and only finitely many are nonzero, by [def-weil-finite-torsion-constructibility] on the coefficient site and by the corresponding bounded constructibility hypothesis in the small etale assertion.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: bounded finite stalk cohomology

proof.text:
On the pro-etale site the geometric stalk is the inverse-image functor of the topos point of [lem-fix-geometric-stalk-topos-point], using its explicitly stated adjunction and finite-limit preservation. For any sheaf of rings $R$, it gives the ringed-topos morphism with target ring $R_{\bar y}$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-topoi-derived-tensor-pullback] to this morphism: exactness of the stalk makes its derived pullback termwise stalk, and the cited theorem supplies K-flat stalk representatives and
$$(F\otimes_R^L G)_{\bar y}\simeq F_{\bar y}\otimes_{R_{\bar y}}^L G_{\bar y}.$$
For $R=\Lambda_Y$, [lem-weil-proetale-constant-sheaf-stalk] identifies $R_{\bar y}=\Lambda$ and $(\underline N_Y)_{\bar y}=N$ for every $\Lambda$-module $N$, without a finiteness condition. Choose $[a,b]$ from [def-weil-finite-tor-amplitude] and apply the formula with $F=M$ and $G=\underline N_Y$. Exactness gives
$$H^r(C\otimes_\Lambda^L N)\cong\mathcal H^r(M\otimes_\Lambda^L\underline N_Y)_{\bar y}=0\quad(r\notin[a,b]).$$
Thus $C$ has finite Tor amplitude.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: pro-etale derived tensor and the Tor interval

proof.text:
On the small etale site use its geometric topos point from [lem-fix-geometric-stalk-topos-point] and the exact functor [prop-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks-exact]. Its ordinary tensor comparison is [lem-pod-etale-stalk-tensor-scalar], clause 1. The general ringed-topos result [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-topoi-derived-tensor-pullback] applies to this point too and gives the comparison for derived tensor. By [lem-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf-geometric-stalk] the stalk of the constant sheaf of an arbitrary $\Lambda$-module $N$ is $N$; the isomorphism is $\Lambda$-linear because it sends $\lambda n$ to $\lambda$ times the germ of $n$. Therefore
$$H^r(C\otimes_\Lambda^L N)\cong\mathcal H^r(M\otimes_\Lambda^L\underline N_Y)_{\bar y}.$$
The small etale Tor-amplitude hypothesis makes the right side zero outside its interval $[a,b]$, for every $N$. This establishes the Tor-amplitude hypothesis over $\Lambda$ for the small etale stalk as well.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph and small etale clause: the etale comparison

proof.text: On each site, step 1 puts $C$ in $D^b(\Lambda)$ with finitely generated (indeed finite) cohomology in a finite interval, and steps 2 or 3 supply finite Tor amplitude in one interval. If a bounded representative is needed for the stated criterion, replace a representative by its good truncation in an interval containing its cohomological support; the natural truncation maps are quasi-isomorphisms since the omitted cohomology groups vanish. Thus the two hypotheses in [lem-trf-finite-tor-amplitude-perfect]—finite cohomology and finite Tor amplitude—hold for the same stalk complex. Apply its only-if direction with $A=\Lambda=A_{E,n}$. Its conclusion is already a bounded complex of finitely generated free modules; no additional projective-to-free theorem is being inferred from a definition. This proves both finite-coefficient assertions.

source.place: Proof, finite coefficients: apply the existing algebraic perfectness criterion

proof.text:
For the rational coefficient assertion, represent $M\in D^b_c(Y,E)$ by an integral object $K\in D^b_c(Y,\mathcal O_E)$ as in [def-weil-rationalization-karoubi]. Put $R=\mathcal O_E$, $\pi=\varpi_E$, $A_j=R/(\pi^j)$, $K_j=K\otimes^L_{\widehat R_Y}(A_j)_Y$, and $C_j=(K_j)_{\bar y}$. By [def-weil-derived-complete-integral-detailed] each $K_j$ is bounded constructible, with a common cohomological interval. Hence step 1 gives bounded finite $A_j$-cohomology for $C_j$. Use one K-flat resolution $P\to K$ with flat terms in [def-weil-integral-derived-reduction] to form all reductions. Change of rings preserves K-flatness by [lem-pur-kflat-change-of-rings], so
$$(P\otimes_{\widehat R_Y}(A_{j+1})_Y)\otimes_{(A_{j+1})_Y}(A_j)_Y=P\otimes_{\widehat R_Y}(A_j)_Y$$
computes derived change of rings. Taking stalks using the comparison of step 2 yields coherent isomorphisms $C_{j+1}\otimes^L_{A_{j+1}}A_j\simeq C_j$; the transition maps are induced by the quotient maps in this single resolution, so their composites agree. More explicitly, set $P_j=P\otimes_{\widehat R_Y}(A_j)_Y$. The quotient maps $P_{j+1}\to P_j$ are maps of complexes of $(A_{j+1})_Y$-modules, with the target viewed by restriction of scalars. Their stalks are therefore $A_{j+1}$-linear chain maps representing $C_{j+1}\to C_j$ in $D(A_{j+1})$. Each $P_j$ is K-flat with flat terms by the cited change-of-rings lemma, and its stalk is K-flat with flat terms by step 2. The displayed termwise tensor identity thus identifies precisely the derived quotient map induced by this transition with an isomorphism, as required in step 8; it is not merely an unrelated isomorphism of the two objects.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph: finite reductions of an integral representative

proof.text: The ring $R$ is $\pi$-adically complete: [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-integers-dvr] identifies $\pi$-powers with valuation bounds and gives $|\pi|<1$, and [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-complete] makes $E$ complete. Lifts $x_j\in R$ of a compatible family modulo $\pi^j$ satisfy $|x_{j+1}-x_j|\leq|\pi|^j$ and converge to a unique element of the closed unit ball $R$, with the prescribed residues. More explicitly, compatibility gives $x_k-x_j\in\pi^jR$ for every $k\geq j$, hence $|x_k-x_j|\leq|\pi|^j$. The balls $\pi^jR=\{z:|z|\leq|\pi|^j\}$ are closed, so the limit $x$ satisfies $x-x_j\in\pi^jR$ for every $j$. Two elements with these residues have difference of absolute value at most $|\pi|^j$ for every $j$, hence are equal. Thus the canonical ring map $R\to\varprojlim_jA_j$ is an isomorphism. By [lem-cbc-proetale-classical-stalk] the pro-etale stalk is evaluation on the strict localization, so it commutes with products and inverse limits of sheaves, which are computed objectwise. Together with [lem-weil-proetale-constant-sheaf-stalk] this gives $(\widehat R_Y)_{\bar y}=\varprojlim_jA_j=R$. Let $C_0=K_{\bar y}\in D(R)$. The derived-completeness triangle of [def-weil-derived-complete] remains a distinguished triangle after this exact stalk functor. Its product terms become $\prod_j C_j$, and its transition endomorphism has $j$-th component $z_j-t_jz_{j+1}$. By [lem-weil-derived-limit-products-core] termwise products compute these derived products (for the source this is built into [def-weil-derived-complete], and products of modules are exact). It follows that $C_0\simeq R\varprojlim_jC_j$. This argument uses evaluation at the pro-etale strict localization, rather than assuming that an etale stalk commutes with countable products. Here products of module sheaves and the completed coefficient sheaf are evaluated on the same strict-localization object. Consequently, for any chosen complexes representing the reductions, stalk applied to their degreewise product is the degreewise product of their stalk complexes, with the stated transition maps. Exactness makes this independent of the chosen representatives and preserves the triangle: applying the stalk termwise preserves the finite direct sums in a mapping cone and its differential. Products of modules are exact because a tuple in the product of quotient modules can be lifted one coordinate at a time; kernels are coordinatewise as well. The hypotheses of the cited derived-product theorem therefore hold for the target module category, while the source degreewise-product model is supplied by the derived-completeness definition.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph: identify the integral fibre with its derived reduction limit

proof.text: The residue ring $A_1$ is a field by [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-integers-dvr]. The complex $C_1$ has bounded finite-dimensional cohomology by step 5. Choose a basis of each nonzero $H^i(C_1)$ and cycle lifts in a representative complex; these define a chain map $\bigoplus_i H^i(C_1)[-i]\to C_1$ inducing the identity on all cohomology groups. The sum is finite and its terms are finite-dimensional, so this map is a quasi-isomorphism and $C_1$ is perfect.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph: split the residue-field complex

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-rlim-perfect-complete] with $A=R$, $I=(\pi)$ and the system $C_j$. Completeness was verified in step 6, the required derived quotient isomorphisms in step 5, and perfectness of $C_1$ in step 7. It follows that $C_0\simeq R\varprojlim_jC_j$ is a bounded complex of finite projective $R$-modules. The rational stalk of the representative $K$ is $C_0\otimes_R E$ by scalar localization [def-weil-rationalization-karoubi]: a localized morphism $f\otimes e$ acts by $f_{\bar y}\otimes e$. Localization $R\to E=R[1/\pi]$ is flat, since localization sends an exact sequence to an exact sequence by the fraction criterion for zero. Thus termwise tensor represents the derived scalar extension. Each term of the perfect model is a direct summand of $R^m$ and becomes a direct summand of $E^m$, hence a finite-dimensional vector space. This is the required bounded finite-dimensional perfect model at stage $E$.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph: reconstruct and rationalize the integral perfect fibre

proof.text: For an object of $D^b_c(Y,\Qlb)$ choose its representative $(E,M_E)$ in [def-weil-algebraically-closed-coefficients]. Step 8 produces a bounded finite-dimensional $E$-complex $V^\bullet$ for its geometric fibre. Its fibre over $\Qlb$ is represented by $V^\bullet\otimes_E\Qlb$. Choosing a basis in each degree identifies its terms with $\Qlb^{\dim_E V^i}$, and the degrees outside the original finite interval remain zero. Tensor over the field $E$ is exact because every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits. Consequently this is a bounded finite-dimensional complex representing the geometric stalk, and proves the common-stage field assertion.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph: extend a finite-field model to the common-stage coefficients
